body: TEMPORARY ASSISTANCE FOR NEEDY FAMILIES (TANF) STATE PLAN EXECUTIVE SUMMARY In May 1996, the Alaska State legislature created the Alaska Temporary Assistance Program (ATAP), which replaced the welfare programs Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) and Jobs, Opportunities and Basic Skills (JOBS). That same year, the federal government enacted the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) of 1996, which provides the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) block grant. ATAP, which is Alaska’s name for the TANF program, was implemented in 1997, is funded through a combination of state funds and TANF block grant. The TANF State Plan (the Plan) is required for Alaska to receive federal block grant funds. The Plan describes major program provisions and outlines eligibility criteria, participation requirements, and program benefits available to participants. All needy Alaskan families with dependent children may apply to participate in ATAP. To qualify, families establish eligibility based on family composition and financial need. To continue participation in the program, parents or caretaker relatives included in the assistance unit must engage in work activities within 24 months of entering the program, in accordance with Title IV-A, section 407 of the Social Security Act. The TANF Block Grant has requirements not found in earlier welfare programs. TANF is time-limited, and families may only receive a total of 60 months of cash benefits in their lifetime unless they qualify for an exemption. ATAP uses an individualized Work First approach to promote family self- sufficiency. Families build on their strengths and actively seek employment, which includes being assigned a case manager and completing a Family Self-Sufficiency Plan (FSSP) and employability assessment for each adult in the household. Families must participate in work activities and cooperate with child support enforcement. Minor teen parents must live with a parent or in another approved living arrangement while they continue their education. ATAP includes cash benefits to help pay for basic living expenses while a family makes progress toward economic independence through employment. Supportive services are available through ATAP case management and may be used to purchase or reimburse the costs of services determined necessary to support work activities such as childcare, transportation and job-related training. ATAP promotes strong partnerships with local governments, Native organizations, non-profit and profit organizations to promote jobs and identify effective community work experience. The Division evaluates ATAP using data-based performance measures of success. These measures include the number of adults employed within 90 days, the number of adults that closed the ATAP case with earnings, the number who leave assistance with employment and do not return, and the number participating in a job development activity. Alaska TANF State Plan Plan Effective December 31, 2025

body: I. INTRODUCTION Alaska enacted a statute in 1996 that provides for a comprehensive family assistance program known as the Alaska Temporary Assistance Program (ATAP). ATAP replaced the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program. In the same year, the federal government enacted the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) of 1996 that provides for the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) block grant. ATAP is funded through a combination of state funds and the federal TANF block grant. This State Plan (the Plan) describes how Alaska's Department of Health (the Department) and Division of Public Assistance (the Division) will operate ATAP and other TANF funded services. The Congressional intent of the TANF block grant was to increase the flexibility of states to fund a variety of services for needy families. Alaska has taken advantage of this opportunity to use TANF funds for services that promote parental responsibility, work, reduce out-of-wedlock pregnancies and encourage the formation of two-parent families. 1. GOALS The overarching goals of ATAP is to move Alaskans from welfare jobs so they can support their families and also to maintain a safety net for those truly in need. 1.1 CENTRAL PRINCIPLES THAT GUIDE ALASKA TOWARD THIS GOAL Emphasize Work Alaska places a strong emphasis on work and job readiness by adhering to the Work First philosophy that employment is both the goal and the expectation for ATAP recipients. Alaska is committed to creating job opportunities for recipients in public and private sectors and emphasizing work. Promote Responsibility Alaska encourages family self-sufficiency and stability through several initiatives promoting individual responsibility. This includes planning for self-support, actively pursuing child support, and prevention of unplanned and out-of-wedlock pregnancies. Set Limits Alaska limits ATAP payments to 60 months for most families and reduces benefits for two-parent families during the summer when work opportunities increase. The state disqualifies the entire assistance unit if a parent refuses or quits a job and penalizes the assistance unit if a parent fails, without good cause, to participate in work and other self- sufficiency activities or fails to cooperate with child support enforcement. Maintain a Safety Net Alaska maintains a safety net for needy children and encourages families to care for their children in their own home. Supports Coordination of Agency Resources Alaska supports efficient and effective use of state and community resources for families receiving services from multiple agencies. Coordination of social service efforts and providing for wrap-around services focused on family integrity, stability, and self- sufficiency allows families experiencing multiple and profound challenges to make meaningful progress towards employment, self-sufficiency, and exiting the program. 2. PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT Alaska is committed to public involvement in program design and implementation. Since program implementation, continued public involvement has been promoted through information sharing and numerous opportunities for public comment. • TANF State Plan: Alaskans are offered a 45-day public comment period prior to the submission of the Plan to ACF for recertification. • Alaska Statute and Administrate Code: Alaskans are offered the opportunity to share public comment prior to revisions. • Community Outreach: Alaska takes advantage of ongoing opportunities to inform and respond to the public through the news media, social media, internet webpages, and participation in various public forums and meetings. All specified avenues of communication provide the public with information and assist with obtaining public opinion and responses to ATAP. body: II. ALASKA TEMPORARY ASSISTANCE MAJOR PROVISIONS 3. ELIGIBLE FAMILIES Families establish program eligibility based on family composition and a determination of financial need that considers the family’s available income and assets. For the purpose of participating in ATAP, eligible families are: • families that include a caretaker relative of one or more related dependent children; • two-parent families in which both parents live in the same household; or • families that include a needy dependent child and a non-needy caretaker relative. 3.1 DEPENDENT CHILD For purposes of eligibility, a dependent child is under 18 years of age. If a child is 18 years of age, he or she may continue to be considered a dependent child if they are a full-time student in a secondary school or in vocational or technical training. Eligibility ends the month of course completion, withdrawal from enrollment, or their 19th birthday, whichever occurs first. 3.2 RESIDENCY To meet the residency requirement, a family must be living in Alaska with the intent of remaining an Alaska resident. The Division does not treat new residents of the state differently than other families with established Alaska residency. 3.3 EQUITABLE ACCESS All families in the state will have equitable access to ATAP benefits; this includes Alaska Native families who are not served by a Native Family Assistance Program (NFAP). There are Division field offices in the majority of Alaska’s urbanized areas and urban clusters as defined by the most recent U.S. Census. Divisions offices are open to the public in the following cities: Anchorage, Bethel, Fairbanks, Homer, Juneau, Kenai, Ketchikan, Kodiak, Nome, Sitka, and Wasilla. All offices have a drop box for recipients to submit applications, review forms, supporting documentation, reports of change, etc. during non-business hours. Office locations, mailing addresses, phone, fax, and email address are listed on DPA’s “Application for Services” form and on DPA’s website at https://health.alaska.gov/dpa. Office hours, email, fax number, and cases statuses via automated message are also available through DPA’s Virtual Contact Center (VCC) at 1-800-478-7778. Email and secure messaging are available for recipients to send questions, submit applications, review forms, supporting documentation, reports of change, etc. Alaska TANF State Plan P lan Effective December 31, 2025 3 | P a g e

The email address is listed on the Division’s “Application for Services” form and via automated message through DPA’s VCC at 1-800-478-7778, and both email and secure messaging addresses are listed on the Division’s website at https://health.alaska.gov/dpa. A fee agent network is active in over two hundred of Alaska’s rural and certain urban communities. Fee agents accept applications for all Alaska public assistance programs. The Division also has an active contract for services with the interpreter service, Language Link Solutions. This 240-language interpreter service empowers Alaska residents to cross the language barrier and seek public assistance. In April 2021, the Division launched a virtual contact center. The Virtual Contact Center (VCC) enables recipients to interact with a live person over the phone from 8 AM – 5 PM, Monday through Friday, excluding State of Alaska observed holidays. Recipients can check the status of an application, ask general questions, and apply and participate in an interview for all public assistance programs from the comfort and convenience of their home. 3.4 NON-CITIZENS Alaska will provide ATAP coverage to otherwise eligible non- citizens classified as “qualified” aliens as defined in 8 U.S.C. 1641. Qualified aliens who arrived in the country prior to the August 22, 1996, enactment of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) may receive assistance immediately upon application for assistance. Qualified aliens who entered the country on or after August 22, 1996, are ineligible for Temporary Assistance for the first five years they reside in the country, unless they are determined to be exempt from the five-year waiting period because of their immigration status (such as a refugee or asylee). In determining eligibility for qualified aliens, a portion of the income and assets of the immigrant’s sponsor are counted. Non-qualified aliens are not eligible for Alaska Temporary Assistance. 3.5 60-MONTH TIME LIMIT Families are not eligible if the family includes an adult who has received 60 months of assistance from ATAP, a TANF-funded program in another state, or a Native TANF- funded program. After 60 months, a family may receive a benefits extension based on hardship if the Division determines the family is unable to become self- supporting because of: • domestic violence; • physical or mental inability to perform gainful activity; • caring for a child or relative who is experiencing a disability; or • other hardship defined by the Division in regulation. body: Time-limit exemptions may not exceed 20 percent of the ATAP caseload. Segregated state TANF funds will be used to provide assistance for families receiving time-limit exemptions beyond the 20 percent maximum allowed under federal law. 3.6 PROGRAM PARTICIPANT RIGHTS The Division’s employee training plans include the topic of ethical conduct and has the Division’s processes on the topic readily accessible via the DPA Administrative Procedures Manual, section 100-10 Ethical Conduct. This manual is available on the Division’s intranet and public website. All ATAP applicants and program participants are provided fair and equitable treatment and have a legal right to a fair hearing. An opportunity for a hearing is granted to any recipient whose application for assistance is denied or whose benefits are altered or terminated. A hearing request can be made in writing either by the recipient or by an authorized representative acting on the recipient's behalf to any Division employee. If requested, the Division will assist the recipient in making a hearing request. A hearing request must be made within 30 days from the date of the notice. The state regulation at 7 AAC 49.010 – 900 further defines the written notice requirements, selection of hearing location, and timelines for these actions. When applicants and program participants request a fair hearing they are provided with the “All About Fair Hearings” (GEN 84) form and the “Preparing for your Fair Hearing” (DPA5) form in order to prepare them for the fair hearing process. These forms are available in hardcopy and ADA compliant electronic copy and can be physically handed, mailed, faxed, or emailed to the applicant or program recipient. A recipient has 10 days to submit written opposition if they disagree with the proposed decision. The Department Commissioner or designee will review the proposed decision. Once the Commissioner renders the final decision, it is binding upon the agency. The recipient can still appeal to the Superior Court. Applicants and program participants of ATAP are informed of their rights multiple times throughout the program eligibility determination process and review period. Their program rights and responsibilities along with their civil rights are provided as follows: • Printed on pages 3 – 5 of the Division’s Public Assistance Application (GEN 50C) and on pages 9 – 11 of the Public Assistance Review Application (GEN 72). These forms are available in hardcopy via lobby or upon fax or mail out request and ADA compliant electronic copy via the Division’s public website or upon email request. • Verbally or visually (American Sign Language) reviewed in a language familiar to the applicant or the participant at time of initial application interview, fee agent interview, and at review interview. • Printed on every notice sent by the Division. body: 4. ALASKA TEMPORARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM (ATAP) REQUIREMENTS Eligible families may participate in ATAP provided they fulfill specific obligations. These obligations include providing necessary information about themselves and their family through the program application process, planning for self-sufficiency, and participating in work activities. If they fulfill program requirements, they receive benefits to provide for their basic needs and to assist them in achieving self- sufficiency and exiting the program. 4.1 APPLICATION Application must be made on a form approved by the Division. To be considered complete, the application must provide all requested information and be supported by documentation the Division determines necessary to establish eligibility. The Division will offer assistance to those applicants expressing difficulty with completing the application or obtaining required verification. Completed applications received by the Division will be processed within 30 days of receipt. 4.2 FAMILY SELF-SUFFICIENCY PLAN (FSSP) AND ASSESSMENT Every adult included in a needy family must complete an FSSP. The plan outlines the steps the family will take to increase their independence, identifies specific milestones to indicate progress, and indicates the services the Division will provide to assist the family toward their goals. The family works with a DPA employee or contractor (case manager) to develop their own FSSP. As the first step in developing the FSSP, an assessment of the skills, work experience, and employability (employability assessment) of each parent or caretaker relative who is age 18 or older, or who is not attending secondary school and is without a high school diploma or GED. It is completed within 30 days after a family’s referral to Work Services Case Management by the household’s assigned case manager. 4.3 REPORTING REQUIREMENTS Participants must report to the Division specific changes in their household circumstances that may affect their program eligibility or payment amount. These reports must be made within 10 days of when the parent or caretaker relative knows of the change. There is a five-day reporting requirement if a dependent child is expected to be absent from the home for more than a full calendar month. If failure to report results in overpayment, participants are responsible for repayment to the state. An intentional failure to report a change or a misrepresentation of household circumstances may result in fraud prosecution or an intentional program violation penalty. The parent remains a mandatory filing unit member while absent. 4.5 CHILD SUPPORT Regular child support payments are essential to help most single-parent ATAP families attain and sustain self-sufficiency. Participants are required to cooperate with the Child Support Enforcement Division (CSED) in establishing paternity and establishing, modifying, or enforcing a child support order for a dependent child within the family. This requirement is waived if an applicant or recipient can establish good cause for not cooperating with CSED. Good cause reasons must be approved by the Division. An applicant must assign to the state all rights to child support for months they receive ATAP benefits once the family is eligible for benefits. 4.6 MINOR PARENTS Minor parents are individuals under the age of 18 who are not married or emancipated, and who have applied for ATAP on behalf of themselves and their dependent children. The program requires minor teen parents to follow specific requirements designed to help them be responsible parents and independent adults. Minor parents must live in an adult-supervised setting. They may live with a parent or guardian, another adult relative, or in a setting such as a group home that has been approved by the Department. If a minor parent does not comply with this requirement, the entire family is ineligible. Minor parents who do not have a high school diploma or General Education Development (GED) must maintain an adequate level of school attendance in a secondary school or other appropriate training program. An adequate level of school attendance is one that meets the program’s graduation or certification requirements. If a minor parent does not comply with this requirement, the family’s benefit is reduced. 4.7 PENALTIES AND SANCTIONS An otherwise needy family may not participate in the ATAP if it is specifically excluded by law. A participating family may have benefits reduced for failure to fulfill program requirements. Families are ineligible for TANF funded ATAP benefits when: • The family includes an adult who fraudulently misrepresented their residence in order to receive TANF-funded benefits in more than one state. The family is ineligible for 10 years beginning at the date of conviction. • The family includes an individual who is determined to be fleeing to avoid prosecution, custody, or confinement after conviction for a crime that is classified as a felony or a class A misdemeanor. body: III. WORK AND SELF-SUFFICIENCY The Division has implemented work and self-sufficiency programs that promote job creation, provide the recipient with job preparation and provide job support services designed to help recipients gain and retain paid employment. Alaska regularly evaluates the effectiveness of these programs through data-based performance measures of program results. The Division conforms to the work participation rates required by TANF rules. Child-only cases are not considered in the participation rate calculation. Federal statute establishes work participation rates of 50 percent for all families and 90 percent for two-parent families. Actual required participation rates may be reduced through applicable federal caseload reduction credits authorized under federal law. 5. WORK SERVICES DELIVERY The Division uses an employment focused approach to providing services to connect ATAP families to work and the goal of self-sufficiency. The Division encourages all interested and eligible ATAP recipients to pursue work in high demand occupations by working closely with their work services case managers and providing supportive services to assist recipients train for, seek, and maintain these opportunities on an individualized basis. ATAP program participants are trained for high demand occupations when they show interest and capacity for a field during the employability assessment process. Appropriate referrals are made to training organizations to assist the participants in acquiring the training needed to enter the emergent employment opportunities. The need for skilled direct care, elder care, and long-term care facility staff continues in Alaska. Recipients are screened for interest and capacity for the work during their intake and self- sufficiency planning process. Those without barrier crimes who show interest and capacity for the work are referred to resources for training and job placement in the field. WORK ACTIVITIES ATAP refers mandatory caretaker relatives to a Work Services provider promptly to develop an FSSP and rapidly engage in assigned work activities. Work activities include: • Unsubsidized employment, including self-employment; • Subsidized public or private sector employment; • Work search; • Vocational Counseling; • On-the-job-training; • Job readiness activities; • Vocational education and training; • Approved community work experience • Approved business work experience; • Job skills training directly related to employment; • Education directly related to employment; and • Culturally appropriate subsistence activities.

7. WORK ACTIVITY EXEMPTIONS A parent or caretaker relative may be exempt from the requirement to participate in work activities because they are: • Needed in the home to care for a disabled relative; • Determined to have a medical condition that limits their ability to participate in work activities; • A caretaker of a child age 12 months or younger, however this exemption has a cumulative 12-month lifetime limit; • A victim of domestic violence; or • Living in a community without available childcare for a child under age 6. Individuals may be referred to other programs or agencies for special services such as vocational rehabilitation, counseling, substance abuse treatment, or other medical services as needs are identified. The Division is not implementing the federal option that requires an exempt parent or caretaker to participate in community work experience activities after two years of benefit receipt. The state chose to opt out of this provision because mandatory participation after two years of assistance may interfere with time spent on activities that will assist the participant to gain early paid employment. Childcare is available when a childcare provider is in the community where the parent lives or participates in their work activities and the provider’s hours of operation meet the parent’s needs. Childcare is appropriate when the childcare provider: • Has the ability to provide safe and competent care for children of the same age and development level as the participant’s children, • Is willing to care for the child(ren), and • Is located within 30 minutes travel time by public or private transportation from the parent’s home or activity site. PROGRAM ASSESSMENT The Division uses a variety of methods to assess and evaluate how well the Division meets the goal of moving Alaskans into jobs so they can support their families. 9.1 ADMINISTRATIVE DATA Work Services: The Division uses specific data-based performance measures to determine program effectiveness. These measures include an ongoing assessment of program success using the federally mandated work participation rates. Other measures include: • Percent of adults employed within 90 days; • Percent of cases that close with earnings; • Percent of cases that close and do not reopen; and • Percent of cases participating in a job development activity. ATAP data is gathered through the Division’s eligibility information system. Ongoing system enhancements are made to evaluate the effectiveness of program policies and to monitor the attainment of regional goals. The Department uses longitudinal data based on evaluation of individual family progress towards safety, stability, and self- sufficiency to measure program efficiency. Over time the total number of families making progress towards family health, stability, and ability to work is used to determine if program strategies and services are successful in moving parents towards self-sufficiency and employment. 10. INITIATIVES TO SUPPORT WELFARE TO WORK 10.1 ALASKA WORKFORCE INVESTMENT BOARD The Alaska Workforce Investment Board (AWIB) is focused on developing a workforce system that is useful, accessible, and understandable to businesses looking for qualified workers, unemployed Alaskans looking for jobs, and incumbent workers wanting to upgrade their skills in a changing work environment. The board provides policy oversight of state and federally funded job training and vocational education programs. These offices provide job seekers, including ATAP recipients, with professional and convenient resources to help them find work. Key agencies include the Divisions of Public Assistance, Employment Security and Vocational Rehabilitation, other Workforce Innovation Opportunity Act (WIOA) agencies and local non-profit organizations. 11. The Division recognizes that local knowledge and resources must be used to place recipients into jobs or other meaningful work activities. The Division collaborates and contracts with community agencies for delivery of some services and purchases others through service agreements. Partnerships between the Division field staff and community agencies are forged at the local level.

body: IV. ALASKA TEMPORARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM (ATAP) BENEFITS Financial eligibility for ATAP is based primarily on family resources and income. Other family economic considerations include childcare, shelter costs, and the number of dependent children living in the home. ATAP payments are intended to help with basic living expenses and are calculated on a monthly basis. Eligibility is reviewed periodically and redeterminations are made whenever a change in family circumstances is reported. 12. FAMILY NEED The Division determines which individuals in the household are members of the ATAP economic unit. The Division establishes: • With whom the dependent child lives; • Who, of the individuals living with the dependent child, is responsible for the child and if their income and resources are available to the child; • If the child is financially needy; and • If any of the individuals in the household are legally or financially responsible for the dependent child’s caretaker relative. Financial need is determined to exist if the family resources and income are below the need standards set by the Department in regulation. There are four sets of need standards used to determine if a family is eligible to receive ATAP based on the composition of the family unit. The tables used to apply these standards are attached to this plan as Appendix A. These standards are adjusted each year by a percentage increase equal to the cost-of-living percentage increase in Social Security Insurance benefits. 12.1 RESOURCES ATAP rules allow families to keep up to $2,000 in assets, or $3,000 if the assistance unit includes an individual who is 60 years of age or older. Program rules will exclude the value of a vehicle that is necessary for family transportation, to participate in work or an approved work activity, as a family’s home, or to transport a disabled family member. The equity value of any non-exempt vehicles will be counted as part of the resource limit. 12.2 EARNED INCOME DEDUCTIONS As an incentive to employment, ATAP allows an earned income deduction when determining a participant’s payment amount. The earned income deductions are designed to encourage work and to ease the transition from assistance to paid employment. body: ensure seamless childcare services for families as they work to achieve economic self- sufficiency. Childcare costs associated with work, approved education and training, community service or other paid and non-paid work activities are paid for through the PASS program. PASS is a three-tiered program that provides seamless childcare subsidies as recipients move from ATAP toward self-sufficiency. To participate in any PASS program, a parent must be working, attending school or training program, or participating in activities assigned on their FSSP. PASS I is funded through TANF and is available for ATAP families engaged in work, job readiness or activities necessary to achieve self-sufficiency. PASS II is funded by TANF and the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) and is available for up to twelve months for transitional purposes for those employed ATAP families whose case closes. The PASS III program is funded by CCDF and provides subsidized childcare for qualifying low- income families. PASS II and PASS III families must be engaged in work, education, or training activities and require a family contribution toward the cost of childcare based on a sliding fee scale depending on a family’s gross income and family size. Provider recruitment and referrals for childcare are accomplished primarily through Alaska’s statewide Resource and Referral Network. Alaska requires that all childcare providers who participate in the PASS program be state or Municipality of Anchorage licensed, state approved, or certified by the United States Department of Defense or United States Coast Guard. Tribally Approved or Tribally Certified providers with standards that meet or exceed the State of Alaska’s standards are also eligible to participate in the PASS program. 14. The manual section is also accessible online. The Division has restricted the use of ATAP benefits from Quest cards (via ATMs or POS devices) at liquor stores, bars, gambling establishments, and adult entertainment establishments. The Division partners with the Department of Commerce, Community and Economic Development to identify businesses where ATAP funds cannot be spent. The Division collaborates with Fidelity National Information Services, Inc. (FIS) to notify ATAP recipients and relevant businesses throughout Alaska, of federal statute P.L. 112-96, and the associated compliance requirements. The Division monitors Quest card ATM transactions monthly at applicable businesses statewide. Additionally, applicants and recipients are informed of these restrictions through language included on applications for services, eligibility review forms, and notices of action, as well as signage for district offices, and posting information on the Division’s website. body: V. PARENTAL RESPONSIBILITY Alaska’s ATAP programs promote parental responsibility. ATAP incorporates child support, minor parent program requirements, and program non-compliance penalties as previously described. Other efforts to promote parental responsibility are described under Other TANF Funded Services. In addition, as a companion to ATAP, Alaska enacted in 1996 and reauthorized in 2001 child support provisions intended to strengthen families and promote parental responsibilities. These provisions include: • Parents of unmarried minor parents may be ordered by a court to pay child support for their grandchild until the minor parent becomes an adult. • The interest rate on child support arrearages is reduced from 12% to 6% to encourage delinquent obligors to comply. • Occupational and driver’s licenses of obligors who are three or more months in arrears on their child support payments are withheld unless the obligors make arrangements with the CSSD. • Alaska’s participation in the National Registry of Child Support Cases and a National Directory of new hires to support the interstate enforcement of child support. VI. NATIVE FAMILY ASSISTANCE Native American Tribes may administer family assistance programs under their own TANF block grants. Federal law specifically names the twelve regional Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act non- profit organizations and the Metlakatla Indian Community as eligible federal block grant recipients in Alaska. These organizations can receive block grants under the Tribal Family Assistance Program upon approval of a plan submitted to the Secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (U.S. DHSS). There are currently seven Alaska Native organizations operating TANF- funded Native Family Assistance Programs (NFAPs) in Alaska: Tanana Chiefs Conference (TCC) in interior Alaska; Bristol Bay Native Association (BBNA) in the Bristol Bay region; Cook Inlet Tribal Corporation, Inc. (CITCI) in the Municipality of Anchorage and Mat-Su Valley; the Association of Village Council Presidents in western Alaska (AVCP); the Central Council of Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska (CCTHITA) in southeast Alaska; Kodiak Area Native Association (KANA) in the Kodiak area; and Maniilaq Inc. in the Northwest Arctic region. Legislation passed in Alaska in 2000 and reauthorized in 2005 gave the Division the authority to award grants to certain Alaska Native organizations who develop and operate their own NFAPs. Native organizations use the state grant to augment their federal TANF block grant to deliver services and activities that promote self-sufficiency and enhance the lives of families in their services areas. The Native regional non-profit organizations are community-based with close ties to local economies. These organizations are able to deliver locally based and culturally relevant programs. The state also contracts and grants with Native organizations to provide for the delivery of Native Employment Work (NEW) Services in those areas not served by NFAPs. The Division provides state funds to certain Alaska Native Tribes that have a plan approved by U.S. DHSS and have signed a grant agreement with the Division. More information on NFAPs in Alaska may be viewed at: http://dpaweb.hss.state.ak.us/manuals/NFAP/NFAP_Guide.htm.

VII. OTHER TANF FUNDED SERVICES The Department uses segregated federal TANF funds outside of the ATAP cash assistance program to support programs that serve needy families and advance one or more of the four purposes of the TANF block grant. These purposes are to: a) Provide assistance to needy families so that children may be cared for in their own homes or in the homes of relatives; b) End the dependence of needy parents on government benefits by promoting job preparation, work, and marriage; c) Prevent and reduce the incidence of out-of-wedlock pregnancies and establish annual numerical goals for preventing and reducing the incidence of these pregnancies; and d) Encourage the formation and maintenance of two-parent families.

Under state policy, with the exception of the ATAP cash assistance program, segregated federal TANF funds may be used to assist families whose income is at or below the Alaska PASS Child Care Assistance Program income limits. A child is defined as a youth up through their 25th birthday. Additionally, a child can be temporarily absent from their own home or the home a relative for up to 180 days. 18. TRANSPORTATION The Department supports the development and expansion of transportation options for ATAP participants who are making the transition to work and self-sufficiency. This support is provided through collaborative planning, and by using segregated federal TANF funds to strengthen the capacity of public transportation systems serving ATAP participants in communities where Limited transportation options affect their ability to obtain and maintain employment. Most of the funds are used to match federal grants awarded to community organizations that provide transit and paratransit services. Additional funds are used to arrange transportation for individual ATAP recipients when necessary to support participation in work activities or employment. The Division encourages and supports local transportation initiatives developed by communities to address their unique transportation challenges. 19. PREGNANCY PREVENTION The Division provides a grant to the Alaska Division of Public Health’s Adolescent Health Program to educate teens and young adults (both male and female) on the problems and risks associated with unintended teen pregnancies. The program works with community organizations to provide education about preventing pregnancies, clinical services, building self-esteem and awareness, and positive youth development activities across 30 communities in Alaska. The goal is to reduce the number of these pregnancies as a means to improve the family’s opportunities to achieve self-sufficiency. The Department collaborates with community partners to provide education, especially to teens, on the problems and risks associated with out-of-wedlock and teen parent pregnancies. In areas of the state with high teen and out-of- wedlock pregnancies and high numbers of unintended pregnancies, efforts are focused on improving access to family planning services and long-term contraceptives for at-risk teens and women. In conjunction with pregnancy prevention efforts, the Department provides education to the public on statutory rape and basic training to community partners on identifying and reporting incidences of statutory rape. Division staff actively seek opportunities to engage and participate with a variety of local and state partners. Many of our Work Services contractors have direct relationships with local and federal law enforcement agencies to address issues such as domestic violence and human trafficking. The Division also maintains multiple provider agreements with adult education providers. The State, using non-TANF funding, supports programs designed to reach Alaska services systems, families and individuals statewide to promote healthy relationships, children and families. The wide range of activities encompasses work to support reduction of teen and out- of-wedlock pregnancy through reducing statutory rape, sexual assault and domestic violence. Efforts promote respect, healthy relationships, and safety for all Alaskans. 20. SERVICES FOR REFUGEE FAMILIES Refugee families new to Alaska often encounter multiple barriers to employment and self- sufficiency including language, culture, health, transportation and basic navigation of Alaska social and health services. In order to support refugee families receiving ATAP benefits, the Division collaborates with Catholic Social Services, federal Office of Refugee Resettlement- funded service provider in Alaska. Refugee families new to Alaska who receive ATAP are referred to Catholic Social Services for work preparation and placement, English as a second language (ESL) classes and life skills education tailored to their needs. This reduces the number of agencies and programs families must access to receive the support they need to successfully plan for and achieve self- sufficiency through employment and ensures that work services which are relevant and effective are provided to this unique population.

body: VIII. ADMINISTRATION 21. ALASKA STATUTE State statute requires the Division to: • Provide assistance with basic living expenses and self-sufficiency services to needy children and their families; • Determine program standards that provide recipients with incentives to work, participate in financial planning, and opportunities to develop self-sufficiency; • Prepare a state plan to submit to the federal government to assure that federal money is available to the state for operation of ATAP; • Administer the program to assure consistency with federal requirement; • Report to the federal government and state legislature information required to comply with any provisions the federal government determines necessary to ensure correct and verifiable information on the program; • Conduct studies and research in order to evaluate and monitor the effectiveness of the state program; and • Adopt regulations and take actions necessary to implement, interpret, and administer ATAP. 22. DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH ADMINISTRATION OF TANF The Department of Health (the Department) administers ATAP through the Division of Public Assistance (the Division). The organizational structure of the Department and the Division with primary responsibility for the administration of ATAP is attached as an appendix. 23. MAINTENANCE OF EFFORT The State funds a range of activities to meet Alaska’s TANF Maintenance of Effort (MOE) requirements. For the purpose of claiming MOE, Alaska’s defines a child as any individual under the age of 19 and families whose income is at or below the Alaska PASS Child Care Assistance Program income limits. Additionally, a child can be temporarily absent from their own home or the home a relative for up to 180 days. A. The following programs are state funded, providing assistance to households with an eligible child: • Monthly cash assistance payments and child support pass through payments. • Childcare provided to ATAP families participating in work, education, training, or other activities included in the Family Self-Sufficiency Plan. • NFAP grants to eligible Tribal Organizations that administer their own federal TANF or Native Employment Works (NEW) Program, supporting basic assistance payments and other allowable expenditures eligible as MOE. • A percentage of the Department’s administration costs for activities as described in this plan. All families must meet both the non-financial and financial eligibility criteria, including having an income at or below the applicable PASS income limit. Parent(s) must also be employed. B. Additional programs and services that are funded by the Department or with local funds to meet the TANF MOE requirements, include: • Programs targeted towards “at risk” youth – Programs which provide after school programming, mentorship opportunities, summer employment, and other supervised support programs and which provide additional educational opportunities for at-risk youth. In some instances, participants may be given grants or scholarships to attend programming with other organizations. • Food and Nutrition – Programs which provide or support the distribution of emergency food assistance to families. • Housing Assistance – Programs that help prevent homelessness and support families in securing permanent housing. • Employability Training – Education and training programs to build skills and capacity in technology, financial security, and other employment related areas. • Youth and College Scholarships – Scholarships and other financial aid programs which provide opportunities for young adults to attend college or post-secondary programs. • Various United Way programs – Provides financial support to programs that provide a variety of services focused on achieving a TANF goals. Programs are focused on supporting “at-risk” youth and families. • Information and Referral Services – Programs and services which aim to connect people with information and resources about health and human services programs and services available in the community. • Support for Children involved with Child Welfare – Support to help children in foster care remain in their own homes or the homes of relatives. 24. CERTIFICATIONS The State of Alaska will operate a program to provide Temporary Assistance to Needy Families (TANF) so that the children may be cared for in their own homes or in the homes of relatives; to end dependence of needy parents on government benefits by promoting job preparation, work and marriage; to prevent and reduce the incidence of out-of-wedlock pregnancies and establish annual numerical goals for preventing and reducing the incidence of these pregnancies; and encourage the formation of two-parent families. This program is known as the Alaska Temporary Assistance Program or ATAP. In administering and operating a program which provides TANF with minor children under title IV-A of the Social Security Act, the Governor of Alaska, Governor Mike Dunleavy, hereby certifies that: • The Department of Health, Division of Public Assistance, is the agency responsible for administering the ATAP program in Alaska. • Local governments and private sector organizations have been consulted regarding the plan and design of welfare services in Alaska so that services are provided in a manner appropriate to local populations; and these organizations have been provided with a 45- day comment period. • Alaska will operate a Child Support Enforcement program under the State Plan approved under part D. • Alaska will operate a Foster Care and Adoption Assistance program in accordance with part E and will take all necessary actions to ensure that children receiving assistance are eligible for medical assistance under title XIX of the Social Security Act. • Alaska will provide each member of an Indian Tribe who is domiciled in the state and is not eligible for assistance under a Tribal Family Assistance plan approved under Section 412 of the Social Security Act, with equitable access to assistance under the state program funded under this part attributable to funds provided by the federal government. • Alaska has established and enforces standards and procedures to ensure against program fraud and abuse, including standards and procedures concerning nepotism, conflicts of interest among individuals responsible for the administration and supervision of the state Alaska TANF State Plan P lan Effective December 31, 2025 28 | P a g e

The TANF Program provides information about the options available to current and potential beneficiaries; and 2. Case workers and other agency personnel responsible for administering the TANF program are provided with training regarding standards and procedures related to the Family Violence Option. • Alaska will screen for and identify individuals receiving assistance under this part with a history of domestic violence while maintaining the confidentiality of such individuals and refer such individuals to counseling and supportive services. Furthermore, the state will waive, pursuant to a determination of good cause, other program requirements such as time limits for individuals receiving assistance, residency requirements, child support cooperation requirements, and family cap provisions, in cases where compliance with such requirements would make it more difficult for individuals receiving assistance under this part to escape domestic violence or unfairly penalize such individuals who are or have been victimized by such violence, or individuals who are at risk of further domestic violence. • Alaska has established and is enforcing standards and procedures to ensure that applicants and potential applicants for TANF are notified of assistance made available by the state to victims of sexual harassment and survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. • Alaska’s case workers and other agency personnel responsible for administering the TANF program are trained in: the nature and dynamics of sexual harassment and domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking; state standards and procedures relating to the prevention of, and assistance for; individuals who are victims of sexual harassment or survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking; and methods of ascertaining and ensuring the confidentiality of personal information and documentation related to applicants for assistance and their children who have provided notice about their experiences of sexual harassment, domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
